phonemes.desc: Voiced bilabial stop [b], as in English 'bald'; Old Norse initial b is fully voiced.
Short open back unrounded [ɑ], held brief — Old Norse short a, not the long á.
Lateral [l], voiced stop [d], and the syllabic trill [r̩] of the nominative ending; the final r carries its own beat, as in modern Icelandic.

pronunciation.approximation: 'BAHL-dur' — a short open 'ah', the l and d run together, and the final r sounded as a light syllabic trill, as in Icelandic Baldur.

kin.label: Old Norse
kin.form: Baldr, son of Óðinn and Frigg; also a rare poetic common noun, baldr 'lord, prince'.

kin.label: Old High German
kin.form: Phol, the figure paired with Wodan in the Second Merseburg Charm, widely — though not universally — read as Baldr.

kin.label: Old English
kin.form: Bældæg, son of Woden in the Anglo-Saxon royal genealogies, whose first element is the same word.

kin.label: Modern Icelandic
kin.form: Baldur, the name's unbroken living form.

pronunciation.note: Baldr is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized Old Norse form is already plain ASCII — there is no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the ASCII alphabet to lose. The god's fame vastly outruns his name's orthography; only the capital distinguishes the restored form from the input.

domains.title: Light, Beauty, Purity
domains.subtitle: The Best and Fairest of the Æsir
domains.lead: Baldr is the shining son of Óðinn and Frigg — the god Snorri calls simply the best: so fair of face and bright that light itself streams from him, so wise and gracious that his judgments cannot be undone. His hall is Breiðablik, the broad-gleaming, where nothing impure may dwell; his death by the mistletoe shaft is the first grief of the gods and the herald of Ragnarǫk.

cards.name: The Mistletoe
cards.desc: The one shoot too young to swear Frigg's oath — slender, fair, and fatal. From it came the dart that felled the god no weapon could wound.

cards.name: Hringhorni
cards.desc: Baldr's ship, greatest of all ships, launched for his pyre by the giantess Hyrrokkin while the Æsir themselves could not shift it.

cards.name: Draupnir
cards.desc: The drip-gold ring Óðinn laid on the pyre beside his son — the treasure the dead god sent back from Hel as proof the errand reached him.

cards.name: Baldrs Brá
cards.desc: 'Baldr's eyelash' — the whitest of all plants, the daisy, so named because the god's brightness was the measure of whiteness itself.

symbols.name: The mistletoe
symbols.meaning: The overlooked thing that undoes the protected god — young, slender, and unsworn

symbols.name: Hringhorni
symbols.meaning: The greatest of ships, built for the voyage he never took and burned as his bier

symbols.name: Draupnir
symbols.meaning: The ring that travels from pyre to Hel and back — love's token across the boundary of death

symbols.name: Breiðablik
symbols.meaning: The broad-gleaming hall where nothing unclean may be — purity made architecture

symbols.name: Baldrs brá (the daisy)
symbols.meaning: The whitest plant in the world, named for his eyelash — brightness as the standard of measure

mythology.lead: Baldr has the thinnest dossier and the heaviest role of any god in the Edda: he acts in almost nothing, and his death sets everything in motion. The sources agree on the shape — the dreams, the oath, the mistletoe, the blind brother's throw, the burning ship, the failed ransom, the promised return — and almost nothing else about him survives at all.

myths.title: The Best and Fairest
myths.text:
Snorri introduces him in the catalogue of the Æsir with a formula the tradition never varies: Baldr the Good, second son of Óðinn, and 'he is the best, and all praise him'. He is so fair of face and bright that a splendour radiates from him, and one plant is so white that it takes its name from his eyelash — baldrs brá, the daisy, whitest of all plants. He is the wisest of the Æsir, the most beautifully spoken, and the most merciful — yet Snorri adds the one shadow across the portrait: none of his judgments holds; nothing he decides can stand.

His dwelling is Breiðablik, the broad-gleaming, and Grímnismál says of that land that the fewest bale-runes lie there — the place in heaven where impurity has least footing. The Edda paints the perfect god first so that everything after reads as loss.

myths.title: The Dreams and the Prophecy
myths.text:
It begins with dreams. Baldr dreams baleful dreams for his life, and the Æsir take counsel. In Baldrs draumar — the whole poem is this one episode — Óðinn himself saddles Sleipnir, rides down the dark road to Niflhel, and raises a dead völva from her grave east of Hel's gate with spells. She answers unwilling: the benches of Hel are strewn and shining, the mead brewed — for Baldr. Höðr will be his slayer; Váli, born to Óðinn, will avenge him one night old, unwashed and uncombed until he brings Baldr's foe to the pyre. And at the end she names the refusal to come: Þökk will weep dry tears for the burning; let Hel hold what she has.

Völuspá gives the same knowledge to its seeress: 'I saw for Baldr, the bleeding victim, Óðinn's child, what was fated.' The mistletoe stood slim and very fair, high-grown — and from that slender shoot came a dangerous dart of sorrow, and Höðr shot it. Baldr's death is the only event in the Edda told as prophecy before it is told as history: the gods know, and it happens anyway.

myths.title: The Oath and the Mistletoe
myths.text:
Frigg takes the foreseen answer and fights it: she travels the world and exacts an oath from all things — fire and water, iron and every metal, stones, earth, trees, sicknesses, beasts, birds, poison, serpents — that they will not harm Baldr. Only the mistletoe, growing west of Valhǫll, seemed too young to demand the oath of. When this was done, the gods' pastime at the assembly was to stand and shoot at Baldr, hurl stones, strike him — and nothing hurt him, and all thought it a great glory.

Loki, Snorri says, could not bear it. In a woman's shape he drew from Frigg the single omission, pulled up the mistletoe, and put it in the hand of Höðr, Baldr's blind brother, who stood at the edge of the circle because he could see nothing and had no weapon. 'Do as the others do,' Loki said; 'I will show you where he stands.' Höðr threw, and the shaft went through Baldr, and he fell dead to the earth — 'the most ill-fated deed,' Snorri writes, 'done among gods and men.' The Æsir could not even take vengeance there, in the sanctuary; they could only weep, and when they found their voices, Frigg asked who would ride to Hel to ransom him.

myths.title: Hringhorni and the One Refusal
myths.text:
The Æsir carried Baldr to the sea and brought out Hringhorni, his ship, the greatest of all ships, meaning to give him a pyre at sea — and they could not move it. A giantess named Hyrrokkin was summoned from Jötunheimr, riding a wolf with vipers for reins, and she launched the ship with one shove so that fire flew from the rollers and the lands quaked. On the pyre they laid Baldr, and when Nanna, his wife, daughter of Nepr, saw him, her heart burst with grief and she was laid on the fire beside him. Óðinn laid the ring Draupnir on the pyre; Þórr hallowed it with Mjölnir, and as he did he kicked the dwarf Litr, who ran before his feet, into the flames.

Then comes the errand every Norse listener knew by heart: Hermóðr rode nine nights to Hel and begged her to let Baldr go, and Hel set the condition — if all things in the world, living and lifeless, weep for him, he shall return. Messengers went through all the world, and all things wept: men and beasts, earth and stones, trees and every metal — 'as you have surely seen these things weep when they come from frost into warmth'. Only one giantess in a cave, who called herself Þökk, Thanks, wept dry tears: 'Let Hel hold what she has.' The Æsir believed Þökk was Loki. Baldr stayed, and the gods' first grief became the first certainty of Ragnarǫk.

myths.title: Balderus and Høtherus
myths.text:
Saxo Grammaticus, writing a generation before Snorri's Edda reached its final form, tells the same death as Danish heroic history. His Balderus is a demigod, son of Odin, whose body no ordinary steel can wound; his rival is not a blind brother but a human prince, Høtherus, and they contend not in a game at the assembly but for the hand of Nanna, whom Høtherus loves and Balderus covets. The supernatural edge of the Edda survives in fragments: Høtherus wins from the wood-satyr Mimingus the sword Mimming and a bracelet; strange forest maidens give him food that steals the gods' strength; and when at last Høtherus wounds Balderus, the demigod lingers three days, dies, and is buried in a barrow. Vengeance follows the old pattern: Bous — Saxo's form of Váli — son of Odin and Rinda, is begotten for the purpose and kills Høtherus, dying himself of his wounds.

Where Snorri's Baldr is innocence murdered by malice, Saxo's is a lover destroyed by rivalry — the euhemerized reading strips the myth of its cosmic grief and keeps its skeleton: the invulnerable man, the one weapon that can harm him, the rival's hand, the begotten avenger. The two accounts are the tradition's own proof that the Baldr story was old, northern, and told in more than one key.

lore.syncretism: The strongest cross-border witness is the Second Merseburg Charm, preserved in a tenth-century Fulda manuscript and the only pagan theogonic text in Old High German: 'Phol and Wodan rode to the wood; then Balder's foal wrenched its foot' — and Wodan charms it whole, bone to bone and blood to blood. Since Jacob Grimm, Phol has widely been read as Baldr himself, which would make the charm the one continental attestation of the god — though the identification is argued, not proven, and Simek counsels caution. The deeper syncretic debate is modern: nineteenth-century scholars, struck by the innocent god who dies and returns after the world's end, read Baldr as a northern Christ or a Frazerian dying-and-rising vegetation spirit. Current scholarship is cooler — Lindow and Orchard note that Baldr's return is scheduled strictly after Ragnarǫk, and that the myth's true company is not the Gospels but the northern complex of fratricide, failed ransom, and prophesied loss.
lore.culturalLegacy: Baldr's afterlife is outsized precisely because his dossier is thin: the beautiful dead god became a vessel every age refills. Matthew Arnold's narrative poem 'Balder Dead' (1855) made him the Victorian emblem of vanished perfection; Frazer's 'Balder the Beautiful' volumes of The Golden Bough built a whole theory of dying gods on the mistletoe; and the Norse revival cast him as the North's own god of light. Modern Heathenry keeps him at the centre of its midsummer and funerary rites as the god of the good death and the return. The name never died in the North itself: Icelandic Baldur and Danish-Norwegian Balder remain living given names, and the daisy — baldrs brá — still carries his eyelash in the Old Norse lexicon.
lore.extendedMeditation: Baldr is the god the Edda built out of an absence. He is given no adventure, no trial, no weapon of his own — only perfection, prophecy, and the one overlooked thing. The myth's engineering is merciless: Frigg's oath is nearly complete, and nearly is the whole story; the gods' game is nearly harmless, and the mistletoe is nearly a plant; the world's weeping is nearly unanimous. Each near-victory is a door closing. What remains is the strangest consolation in the northern corpus — not rescue, but return: after the fire and the flood of Ragnarǫk, Völuspá says, Baldr and Höðr come back together from Hel, the slain and the slayer reconciled, to a green earth. The Edda does not promise that loss can be prevented. It promises that what was best is not lost from the world for good.
lore.originalScriptNote: The normalized Old Norse form is Baldr — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover; in the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved ᛒᛅᛚᛏᛦ (b-a-l-t-R, the t-rune writing d and ᛦ the final nominative -r). Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: baldr.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

lore.archaeology: Baldr is an almost entirely textual god: no runestone invokes him, no votive deposit names him, and the place-name evidence sometimes claimed for him is insecure. The nearest material witnesses are indirect. Úlfr Uggason's Húsdrápa (c. 983), quoted in Skáldskaparmál, describes the funeral procession — Óðinn, Freyr, Heimdallr, the valkyries, and Hyrrokkin launching the ship — as carved on the panels of Óláfr pái's hall at Hjarðarholt in Iceland, proving the myth's currency in pre-Christian art a generation before conversion. On the continent, the Second Merseburg Charm survives in a tenth-century theological manuscript from Fulda (now Merseburg, Cathedral Library), the only Old High German text that may carry the god's name. The Codex Regius preserves Völuspá and Grímnismál; Baldrs draumar is found only in the fourteenth-century manuscript AM 748 I 4to.
